views.name: movies_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  MID,
  title,
  year,
  rating,
  num_votes
FROM Movie

params.when_to_use: Lookup movie-level attributes for a single movie or a small set of movies by MID (e.g., “What are the title, year, rating, and num_votes for movie MID = 123?”). | Join to other tables/views on MID when you need the canonical movie identity and basic attributes (title, year, rating, num_votes) and you will control aggregations in the downstream query. | Display or export a list of movies at the movie grain (one row per MID) with their basic metadata.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need data at a different grain (e.g., one row per genre, language, country, location, or person-role). movies_core is one row per MID; reusing it for per-genre/per-language questions will silently undercount or double-count unless you join to the appropriate join/aggregation view. WHY: joining without adjusting aggregation will produce incorrect row counts and mis-aggregated metrics. | Do not use when you need aggregated metrics that summarize across movies (e.g., counts of movies per genre, counts of people per movie, aggregated ratings distribution). WHY: movies_core has no grouping/aggregation and will not produce aggregate rows — using it instead of an AGG view will return raw rows and require manual aggregation, risking incorrect grouping keys. | Do not use when you need genre/language/country/location membership or multiplicity for each movie. WHY: movies_core has no genre/language columns; reusing it will lose multi-valued relationships (silent false negatives) unless joined to the corresponding JOIN view. | Do not use when you need counts of genres, people by role, or other precomputed counts. WHY: there are dedicated AGG views (movie_genre_counts, movie_person_counts_by_role); using movies_core and counting joined rows can double-count if joins are not deduplicated. | Do not use when you need ranking, windowed metrics, or running aggregates (e.g., top-N by rating, cumulative votes). WHY: movies_core contains only static attributes; sibling RANK/WIN views provide correct window semantics and precomputed ranks or running sums.
params.comparison: use movie_genres(JOIN) instead when you need one row per (MID, genre) — it has the same MID identity but includes genre membership so you won't lose or misrepresent multi-valued genre relationships. | use movie_languages(JOIN) instead when you need language membership per movie — it provides the language dimension that movies_core lacks. | use movie_countries(JOIN) instead when you need country/location membership per movie — it provides country/location rows rather than a single movie row. | use movie_locations(JOIN) instead when you need filming/location entries per movie — movies_core won't show multiple location rows. | use movie_people_roles(JOIN) when you need the people associated to a movie with their roles (one row per person-role) — movies_core only provides movie-level attributes and not person-role linkage. | use movie_genre_counts(AGG) when you need the number of genres per movie or counts aggregated by genre — it provides pre-aggregated counts and avoids manual GROUP BY errors that can arise from joining movies_core to genres and counting. | use movie_person_counts_by_role(AGG) when you need counts of people by role per movie — it aggregates correctly by role, preventing mis-counting from naive joins. | use movies_rating_rank(RANK) when you need movies ranked by rating (or rank-aware queries) — that view encodes ranking/window functions that movies_core does not. | use movies_running_votes(WIN) when you need running/cumulative vote metrics — it contains windowed calculations that would be cumbersome and error-prone to reproduce from movies_core.

views.description: Normalized movie master rows with canonical key and key measures exposed. Use this as the base movie relation for joins, filtering, and aggregations. | Use for: Top-rated movies by year; Movies with high vote counts; Joining movies to genres/countries/languages/people

views.name: movie_genres
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  M_Genre.MID AS MID,
  M_Genre.GID AS GID,
  Genre.Name AS Name
FROM M_Genre
LEFT JOIN Genre ON M_Genre.GID = Genre.GID

params.when_to_use: Find the genre membership for each movie at the most granular level (one row per movie–genre pair). Example: 'List all genres for movie MID = 123' or 'Return (MID, GID) pairs for every genre assignment'. | Join movie-level data to genre attributes when you need the genre Name alongside the raw movie–genre keys, without aggregating or deduplicating. | Filter by genre (GID or Name) and then return matching movies (or further join other movie-dimension views) while preserving the original movie–genre cardinality.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view when you need one row per movie (movie-level aggregates). Reason: this view is at the movie–genre grain (['MID','GID']) and will produce multiple rows per movie for multi-genre movies, causing over-counting or duplicate movie results. | Do not use this view to compute counts or summaries (e.g., number of genres per movie, number of movies per genre) without adding appropriate aggregation. Reason: the view is not aggregated — aggregations done after selecting from it may double-count if you forget GROUP BY MID or GID as appropriate. | Do not use this view when you need only genre metadata independent of movie assignments. Reason: the view repeats Genre.Name once per movie–genre link rather than representing unique genres (use the base Genre table or a derived distinct genre list instead). | Do not reuse this view as a cohort-defining table when your cohort is intended to be movie-level (one row per movie) because filtering on this view will implicitly apply a movie–genre join and may exclude movies with no genres or include movies multiple times depending on downstream joins. | Do not use this view when you need deterministic exclusion of movies lacking a genre. Reason: the view is derived from M_Genre LEFT JOIN Genre, so a movie with no genre will not appear here at all (M_Genre drives rows); using it as a filter will drop genreless movies unless you explicitly handle missing M_Genre rows.
params.comparison: use movies_core instead when you need canonical movie-level attributes (one row per MID) — movies_core is normalized to the movie grain while movie_genres is a join at the movie–genre grain. | use movie_genre_counts instead when you need aggregated counts like number of genres per movie or number of movies per genre — movie_genre_counts is pre-aggregated (AGG) and avoids manual GROUP BY mistakes that can produce wrong counts from movie_genres. | use movie_languages or movie_countries or movie_locations when your question is about alternate movie dimension membership at their respective grains — they are sibling JOIN views with the same pattern but for different domain dimensions; choose the dimension whose GID-like key matches your analytic objective. | use movie_people_roles or movie_person_counts_by_role when the objective concerns people (cast/crew) counts or role-level aggregations — movie_people_roles is a JOIN at movie–person–role grain while movie_person_counts_by_role is an AGG pre-computed per-role; these avoid mixing genre-based multiplicity with people-based multiplicity.

views.description: Denormalized mapping of movies to genre names. One row per movie-genre pair, preserving movie and genre identifiers and descriptive genre Name. Use when filtering or aggregating by genre. | Use for: Count movies per genre; List genres for a given movie; Top-rated movies within each genre

views.name: movie_languages
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  M_Language.MID AS MID,
  M_Language.LAID AS LAID,
  Language.Name AS Name
FROM M_Language
LEFT JOIN Language ON M_Language.LAID = Language.LAID

params.when_to_use: When you need the normalized language assignments for movies at the row-level: one row per (MID, LAID) pair, with the canonical language name. Example question: “List all language IDs and names associated with movie MID = 123.” | When you are joining movie rows to language metadata and require the raw mapping from M_Language (including movies that have a language row even if Language.Name is NULL). | When you need to de-duplicate or enumerate language assignments before applying your own aggregation or filtering (e.g., counting distinct LAID per movie).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to answer questions aggregated at the movie level (one row per MID) without first aggregating: the view’s grain is (MID, LAID). Reusing it directly in aggregations (e.g., COUNT(*) grouped by MID) will count language-rows, not movies — yielding overcounts when movies have multiple languages. | Do not use this view as a movie-cohort filter that expects every movie to appear exactly once: movies with multiple language rows will appear multiple times, and movies with no M_Language rows will not appear at all (LEFT JOIN is from M_Language to Language, so absence of M_Language means absence from this view). This can silently drop or duplicate movies in downstream analysis. | Do not use this view when you need language information restricted to a particular role/cohort or to a different relationship (for example, primary language vs secondary) — this view has no columns distinguishing type/role of the language assignment, so mixing it in will conflate all M_Language rows. | Do not use this view for existence checks that expect complete Language metadata: Language.Name can be NULL if the Language table lacks that row; the LEFT JOIN ensures M_Language rows survive even without matching Language entries, which may silently yield NULL names.
params.comparison: use movies_core instead when you need a single row per movie (one-row-per-MID) — movies_core has the normalized movie-level attributes and avoids the multi-row-per-movie grain of movie_languages. | use movie_genres instead when you are analyzing movie categorical assignments with a similar (MID, categoryID) grain — both are JOIN-type mapping tables, but use movie_genres for genre-specific logic and movie_languages for language-specific logic. | use movie_genre_counts or movie_person_counts_by_role when you need pre-aggregated counts per movie — those sibling AGG views already handle the per-movie aggregation that movie_languages leaves to downstream queries. | use movie_people_roles when you need person-role relationships for people associated with a movie — that sibling is a JOIN mapping at (MID, person-role) grain; do not substitute movie_languages for person-role mappings as they represent different relationship types. | use movies_running_votes or movies_rating_rank when your question involves ranking or windowed aggregates over movies — those sibling RANK/WIN views provide pre-computed rankings/partitions at the movie-level rather than language-row level.

views.description: Denormalized mapping of movies to language names. One row per movie-language pair, preserving movie and language identifiers and descriptive language Name. | Use for: Movies by language; Counts of movies per language; Filter movies by language and year

views.name: movie_countries
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  M_Country.MID AS MID,
  M_Country.CID AS CID,
  Country.Name AS Name
FROM M_Country
LEFT JOIN Country ON M_Country.CID = Country.CID

params.when_to_use: Find the pairings of movie and country at the row level — e.g., list all (MID, CID) associations for movies and their country names. | Return the country name for each movie-country link when you already intend one row per (MID, CID) (the view’s grain). | Join this view into queries that need country metadata for a known movie-country relationship (for example, when you have MID and CID keys and need Country.Name).
params.when_not_to_use: When you need one row per movie (MID) only — this view is at the (MID, CID) grain and will duplicate movie-level data if a movie has multiple countries. Using it will silently overcount or inflate result sets. | When you need one row per country (CID) only — this view is keyed by (MID, CID); aggregating to country-level without DISTINCT or proper aggregation will miscount rows. | When you need to restrict to a single country per movie (e.g., primary country) — the view exposes all linked CIDs; reusing it without applying a specific filter will return multiple countries per movie and produce incorrect cohorts. | When you need aggregated counts (e.g., number of countries per movie) — this is a detail-level JOIN, not an aggregation. Using it directly for counts can produce overcounting unless you wrap it in an aggregation (COUNT(DISTINCT CID) or GROUP BY MID). | When you need to filter by attributes that exist only on the Country table but expect rows for movies that lack country links — this view is a LEFT JOIN from M_Country to Country, so rows come from M_Country; movies without M_Country entries are not present. Reusing it to represent all movies will omit movies with no M_Country rows.
params.comparison: use movies_core(NORM) instead when you want one canonical movie row (movie-level attributes, single-row-per-MID) — movies_core has movie-normalized columns and a movie grain, whereas movie_countries is at (MID, CID) and will return multiple rows per movie. | use movie_genres(JOIN) instead when you are combining movie-level joins of similar many-to-many relationships and want consistent handling across genre-like joins — movie_countries has the same join pattern (link table to dimension) but differs in that both are many-to-many; pick the sibling whose semantic domain (genres vs countries) matches your filter to avoid mixing domains incorrectly. | use movie_genre_counts(AGG) or movie_person_counts_by_role(AGG) when you need aggregated counts per movie — those siblings already provide aggregation at the movie grain, while movie_countries is a raw join and requires explicit aggregation to avoid mis-counts. | use movie_locations(JOIN) or movie_languages(JOIN) when your logic expects a similar join pattern but a different domain — these siblings share the JOIN pattern (link table to dimension) but return different attribute sets (location or language) so choose the sibling matching the domain you intend.

views.description: Denormalized mapping of movies to country names. One row per movie-country pair, preserving movie and country identifiers and descriptive country Name. | Use for: Films produced in a given country; Count movies per country; Top-rated movies by country

views.name: movie_locations
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  M_Location.MID AS MID,
  M_Location.LID AS LID,
  Location.Name AS Name
FROM M_Location
LEFT JOIN Location ON M_Location.LID = Location.LID

params.when_to_use: List every location (LID) associated with a specific movie (MID) — e.g., “show all filming/set locations for movie MID = 123.” | Return the human-readable name for each movie–location pair — e.g., “for each (MID, LID) pair, show Location.Name.” | Joins where you need the one-to-many relationship rows between movies and locations at the raw (MID, LID) grain without aggregation or deduplication.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need a single row per movie (aggregate/deduplicate locations) — this view is at the (MID, LID) grain and will produce multiple rows per MID; using it where a movie-level row is expected will cause overcounting or duplicate movie contributions. | When you need counts of locations per movie — this is not aggregated; using it directly for counts will require an explicit GROUP BY COUNT(LID) or you will get wrong/ambiguous results. | When you need only movies that have at least one location (inner-join semantics) — this view uses LEFT JOIN so movies with NULL Location.Name (or where Location row missing) are preserved; using it as if it were an inner join may silently include movies without valid Location rows. | When you need location attributes other than Name or additional movie attributes — the view only exposes MID, LID, Name; relying on other columns will cause missing-column errors or require rejoining base tables. | When you need a specific cohort/filter applied at the movie level (e.g., only released movies, specific year) — this view applies no movie-side filters, so downstream code must apply them; failing to do so may include unintended movies. | When you need normalized/denormalized movie core fields together (e.g., title, release date, primary key canonicalization) — use a movies_core-style view instead; reusing this view for that purpose would give incomplete movie metadata.
params.comparison: use movies_core (NORM) instead when you need one canonical, movie-level row with normalized core movie fields — movies_core is focused on movie-level attributes, while movie_locations is a (MID, LID) join table returning location rows. | use movie_genres (JOIN) instead when you are working with genre membership at the same MID grain — movie_genres is a sibling join table for genres; prefer it when your logic is about genres rather than locations, because both are join-style but represent different relationship domains. | use movie_genre_counts (AGG) when you need aggregated counts per movie (e.g., number of genres) — similarly, if you need number of locations per movie, aggregate movie_locations rather than treating it as a movie-level view. | use movie_person_counts_by_role (AGG) or movie_people_roles (JOIN) depending on whether you need counts or raw role rows — these illustrate the distinction between JOIN (row-level relationship like movie_locations) and AGG (movie-level aggregated) views; pick the same pattern for locations when appropriate. | use movies_running_votes (WIN) or movies_rating_rank (RANK) when you need ranking/analytic semantics — those sibling views apply analytical transformations at the movie level, unlike this join table which conveys raw relationship rows.

views.description: Denormalized mapping of movies to location names. One row per movie-location pair, preserving movie and location identifiers and descriptive Location Name. | Use for: Movies filmed in a given location; Count filming locations per movie; Filter movies by location and year

views.name: movie_people_roles
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  M_Cast.MID AS MID,
  M_Cast.PID AS PID,
  Person.Name AS Name,
  'cast' AS role
FROM M_Cast
LEFT JOIN Person ON M_Cast.PID = Person.PID
UNION ALL
SELECT
  M_Director.MID AS MID,
  M_Director.PID AS PID,
  Person.Name AS Name,
  'director' AS role
FROM M_Director
LEFT JOIN Person ON M_Director.PID = Person.PID
UNION ALL
SELECT
  M_Producer.MID AS MID,
  M_Producer.PID AS PID,
  Person.Name AS Name,
  'producer' AS role
FROM M_Producer
LEFT JOIN Person ON M_Producer.PID = Person.PID

params.when_to_use: List all person-role assignments for movies: return one row per (MID, PID, role) with the person's name — e.g., “which people were involved in movie X and in what role (cast/director/producer)?” | Unpivoted membership for joins: join movie_people_roles to Movie or other movie-level tables when you need to filter or group by an individual person or by role at the (MID, PID, role) grain. | Enumerating contributors across all role types without deduplication: build a complete roster of all cast, directors, and producers where duplicate PIDs across role types should appear separately (because role is part of the grain). | Feeding row-level downstream processing that expects one record per person-per-movie-per-role (e.g., exporting participant lists, building edges for person→movie graphs labeled by role).
params.when_not_to_use: As a movie-level profile (one row per MID) — it is at the (MID, PID, role) grain, so aggregating without explicit DISTINCT/aggregation will overcount or produce multiple rows per movie. | To get a unique list of people for a movie (de-duplicated across roles) — the view repeats a PID if the same person has multiple roles; using it directly will duplicate that person unless you explicitly deduplicate. | For correct role counts per movie without aggregation — the view is not pre-aggregated; counting rows directly will count each role-instance row (e.g., the same person counted multiple times if they hold multiple roles). | To obtain people linked to movies with additional person attributes that are NULL-intolerant — the LEFT JOIN to Person preserves M_* rows even if Person is missing; downstream consumers that assume Name is non-NULL may be surprised. | When you need to ensure no duplicate rows across source tables — UNION ALL is used, so if the same (MID, PID, role) appears in multiple source tables (unlikely for different role literals but possible via data issues), duplicates are preserved; do not reuse when de-duplication is required without an explicit DISTINCT or aggregation.
params.comparison: use movie_person_counts_by_role instead when you need per-movie aggregated counts of people by role — movie_person_counts_by_role is an AGG at the movie+role level, while movie_people_roles is row-level (MID, PID, role). | use movies_core when you need a single row per movie with core movie attributes — movies_core is normalized movie-level data (one row per MID), whereas movie_people_roles is many-rows-per-movie and will require aggregation to become movie-level. | use movie_genres / movie_languages / movie_countries / movie_locations when you want other many-to-one movie attributes unpivoted by those domains — those sibling JOIN views have a similar pattern (one row per MID per attribute value) but represent different domains (genres, languages, countries, locations) rather than people/roles. | use movie_genre_counts when you need counts of related items per movie (an aggregated metric) — movie_people_roles must be aggregated to produce equivalent counts and will need DISTINCT logic if you want unique people across roles. | use movies_running_votes or movies_rating_rank when your downstream task is ranking or vote-based movie metrics — those siblings are precomputed ranking/aggregation views, unlike the raw membership rows in movie_people_roles.

views.description: Unioned relation of movie-person-role membership across cast, directors, and producers. One row per (movie, person, role) preserving PID and Name and the role label which helps filter by role without joining multiple bridge tables. | Use for: List cast/director/producer for a movie; Find movies for a given person and role; Aggregate counts of distinct people by role per movie

views.name: movie_genre_counts
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  M_Genre.MID AS MID,
  COUNT(DISTINCT M_Genre.GID) AS genre_count,
  group_concat(DISTINCT Genre.Name) AS genre_list
FROM M_Genre
LEFT JOIN Genre ON M_Genre.GID = Genre.GID
GROUP BY M_Genre.MID

params.when_to_use: Count how many distinct genres are associated with a specific movie ID (MID) — e.g., “For movie 123, how many genres does it have?” | List or display the distinct genre names assigned to each movie (as a comma-separated string) at the movie (MID) level — e.g., showing a movie detail page with its genres. | Build reports or joins that need one row per movie containing its genre_count and genre_list (movie-level aggregation).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need genre counts across a different grain (e.g., per person, per country, per year). This view is aggregated to the movie (MID) grain and will silently produce incorrect results if you need aggregation by another dimension. | Do not use when you need non-distinct counts of genre assignments (e.g., counting duplicate assignments or weighted counts). The view uses COUNT(DISTINCT GID) and will undercount if duplicates should be included. | Do not use when you need genre-level rows (one row per movie–genre). This view collapses genres into a count and a concatenated list, so you lose one-row-per-genre detail. | Do not use when you need genre lists in a specific order or with separators other than the default group_concat behavior. group_concat(DISTINCT Genre.Name) produces an unspecified order and default separator, which can break consumers that expect deterministic ordering or a particular delimiter. | Do not use when you need to filter by genre attributes before aggregation (e.g., only count primary genres or only genres with a certain property). The view pre-aggregates all joined genres; applying filters after joining this view will not remove already-aggregated genres. | Do not use when you need to include movies that have no genre rows only under a different join semantics. This view uses a LEFT JOIN from M_Genre to Genre but groups by M_Genre.MID; movies absent from M_Genre (no genre assignments) do not appear here — it will not return every movie from movies_core.
params.comparison: use movie_genres instead when you need one row per movie–genre relationship — movie_genres provides the join-level detail (same base data but not aggregated). | use movies_core instead when you need to list all movies including those with no genres — movies_core is the canonical movie-level table and will include movies missing from M_Genre, whereas movie_genre_counts only contains MIDs present in M_Genre. | use movie_person_counts_by_role when you need analogous person-role counts at a different entity grain — that sibling is also an AGG view but returns counts for persons by role rather than genres by movie, so prefer it for person-role aggregation patterns. | use movie_languages, movie_countries, movie_locations when you need other per-movie aggregated attributes (languages, countries, locations) — these JOIN/AGG siblings may follow different null/duplication semantics, so pick the sibling whose domain (languages/countries/locations) matches your question rather than reusing genre counts.

views.description: Per-movie aggregated counts of how many genres are associated with each movie and a concatenated genre list (when SQLite group_concat is available). Useful to filter multi-genre movies or join a compact genre summary to Movie. | Use for: Find movies with multiple genres; Show genre summary alongside movie metrics; Filter movies by presence/absence of genre membership counts

views.name: movie_person_counts_by_role
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  MID,
  SUM(CASE WHEN role = 'cast' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cast_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN role = 'director' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS director_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN role = 'producer' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS producer_count
FROM (
  SELECT MID, PID, 'cast' AS role FROM M_Cast
  UNION ALL
  SELECT MID, PID, 'director' AS role FROM M_Director
  UNION ALL
  SELECT MID, PID, 'producer' AS role FROM M_Producer
) sub
GROUP BY MID

params.when_to_use: Count how many distinct person-role assignments (by PID) of each specific role exist for a given movie ID (MID). Example: 'For movie MID = 42, how many cast, director, and producer person-rows are recorded?' | Produce a per-movie summary row listing the number of people recorded in each role category, suitable for joining back to a movies table at the movie (MID) grain. | Aggregate queries that need role-specific headcounts per movie (e.g., dashboards, export files) where duplicate person-role rows should be counted as separate entries exactly as they appear in the underlying role tables.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need the number of distinct people (unique PID) per role for a movie — WHY: this view counts each row in the source role tables (M_Cast, M_Director, M_Producer) and will overcount if those tables contain duplicate PID/MID rows; it uses SUM(CASE...) over UNION ALL without deduplicating PIDs. | Do not use when you need to filter or restrict to a cohort of people (e.g., only active people, people of a certain nationality, or people satisfying attributes in a people table) — WHY: the view only contains MID and role counts and loses PID-level detail and any people attributes, so you cannot apply person-level filters without re-joining to the original people tables and re-aggregating. | Do not use when you need counts at a finer grain than MID, such as per-person-per-movie or per-person-role granularity — WHY: the view is aggregated to one row per MID and cannot represent multiple rows per PID or role beyond the summed counts. | Do not use when you need to exclude or deduplicate across roles (for example, count unique people across all roles for a movie) — WHY: the view counts each role separately and will double-count people who appear in multiple role tables. | Do not use when your question depends on source-level nulls, timestamps, or other provenance (e.g., only count entries after a given date or only current role assignments) — WHY: the view materializes unconditional UNION ALL of the three role tables and contains no source timestamps or provenance columns to apply such filters.
params.comparison: use movie_people_roles instead when you need row-level person ↔ movie ↔ role details — it has the PID and role at row-level so you can apply person filters or deduplicate before aggregating, whereas movie_person_counts_by_role is pre-aggregated to MID and loses PID. | use movie_genre_counts instead when you want an example of a properly deduplicated/count-per-MID aggregation for dimensions derived from normalized tables — movie_genre_counts may handle deduplication semantics appropriate to genres, but movie_person_counts_by_role currently uses UNION ALL and will preserve duplicate rows; choose the sibling that matches whether you want UNION ALL semantics or distinct counts. | use movies_core when you need to join core movie attributes (title, release year, etc.) to counts at the movie grain — movies_core provides the movie attributes at the same MID grain so you can safely join, whereas joining to other person- or person-attribute tables from this aggregated view is not possible without losing PID-level control.

views.description: Per-movie counts of distinct people by role (cast, director, producer). Produces one row per movie with separate measure columns for each role count, useful for filtering or correlating movie measures with team sizes. | Use for: Compare movies by size of cast or crew; Filter movies with no directors or multiple producers; Correlate team sizes with ratings

views.name: movies_rating_rank
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  MID,
  title,
  year,
  rating,
  num_votes,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY rating DESC, num_votes DESC) AS year_rating_rank
FROM Movie

params.when_to_use: Rank movies within a single calendar year by their rating (breaking ties by num_votes). Example question: “What are the top-rated movies released in 1995, with their rank within 1995?” | Return one row per movie-year combination where the grouping/ordering should be computed per year (grain is MID + year). | When you need the movie's rating, number of votes, and its dense rank among movies released the same year.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to rank movies across all years (global ranking) — it partitions by year, so ranks restart each year and a global rank would be silently incorrect. | Do not use this view when you need a single row per movie regardless of year (movie-level grain). The view’s grain is MID + year; if Movie contains multiple rows per MID with different years this will produce multiple rows and mis-counts. | Do not use this view to compute ranks within any cohort other than calendar year (for example: decade, genre, language, or director). The PARTITION BY year will give wrong cohorts unless you separately re-partition or re-aggregate. | Do not use this view for aggregations that change the number of movies (filtering/joining prior to ranking). If you JOIN this view to other tables (genres, people, etc.) without first re-computing ranks over the joined set, the rank will reflect the original Movie table, not the filtered/joined cohort — producing silently wrong ranks. | Do not use this view to compute percentile or fractional ranks; it provides DENSE_RANK integer positions only. Consumers expecting percentiles or ties-handling different than dense rank will get incorrect interpretations. | Do not use this view when num_votes or rating needs different tie-breaking rules (it always breaks ties by num_votes descending).
params.comparison: use movies_core(NORM) instead when you need the canonical single-table Movie attributes without any ranking — movies_core provides movie fields without imposing a partition/ordering and is safer for general joins or re-aggregation. | use movie_genre_counts(AGG) or movie_person_counts_by_role(AGG) instead when you need counts aggregated by movie (or by role) to drive ranking cohorts — those siblings provide pre-aggregated counts across joins so ranks over those cohorts will be correct. | use movies_running_votes(WIN) instead when you need running-window aggregates over time (for example, rolling averages or running counts) — movies_rating_rank only computes a per-year dense rank and does not provide running/windowed aggregates across time. | use the JOIN siblings (movie_genres, movie_languages, movie_countries, movie_locations, movie_people_roles) when you need to rank within a subgroup defined by those dimensions — those joins let you create the correct cohort before computing ranks; reusing movies_rating_rank and then joining will not adjust the partitioning and can silently mis-rank.

views.description: Per-year ranking of movies by rating then num_votes. Exposes a dense rank so downstream queries can select top-K per year by applying a rank <= K predicate. Year is preserved as-is (text). | Use for: Top-K movies per year by rating; Find where a movie ranks within its release year; Yearly leaderboards by rating

views.name: movies_running_votes
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  MID,
  title,
  year,
  rating,
  num_votes,
  SUM(num_votes) OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY rating DESC, num_votes DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS year_votes_cume
FROM Movie

params.when_to_use: When you need per-movie (MID) attributes including title, year, rating and the movie's own num_votes for that movie-year combination. | When you need a within-year cumulative sum of votes ordered by rating (descending) and num_votes (descending) up to and including each movie — e.g., 'what is the running total of votes in each year when movies are sorted by rating then votes?' | When the analysis grain is exactly (MID, year) and you do not need any extra joins or additional grouping that would change row multiplicity.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not reuse this view when you need the count of votes for a different cohort (for example, cumulative votes across all years or within a genre/country/language) — the window PARTITION BY year restricts the cumulative sum to the movie's year only, so results would be silently wrong for other cohorts. | Do not reuse this view when you plan to aggregate afterwards across movies (for example, grouping by year to get total votes per year) without removing the per-row num_votes first — num_votes is per-MID and year_votes_cume is a running total per row; aggregating these rows as-is will double-count or mis-count votes. | Do not reuse this view when you need a rank-based ordering independent of rating/num_votes (for example, rank by num_votes only or by an alternate rating metric) — the window ORDER BY is hard-coded to (rating DESC, num_votes DESC) and the cumulative results assume that ordering. | Do not reuse this view when the target grain is movie + role/person/genre/country/etc. Joins to sibling JOIN views (movie_genres, movie_people_roles, etc.) will multiply rows per MID and therefore distort num_votes and year_votes_cume unless you re-aggregate carefully. | Do not reuse this view as a source for percent-of-year totals per grouping (for example, percent of votes in year contributed by a genre) unless you first compute proper denominators at the same cohort level — year_votes_cume is a running cumulative metric, not the per-year total (the final row per year equals the year total, but intermediate rows do not). | Do not reuse this view when you need tie-handling different from rating DESC, num_votes DESC — ties are broken by the second column num_votes; if your tie semantics differ, the cumulative sums will be assigned to different rows.
params.comparison: use movies_core(NORM) instead when you want the canonical per-MID attributes without the running cumulative calculation — movies_core provides the base movie rows and avoids the window-ordering assumptions embedded in movies_running_votes. | use movies_rating_rank(RANK) instead when you need a position/rank of movies by rating within a year rather than a running sum of votes — movies_rating_rank encodes rank semantics (ordering and ties) rather than cumulative vote totals. | use movie_genres(JOIN) / movie_languages(JOIN) / movie_countries(JOIN) when you need cohort-specific vote sums or counts by genre/language/country — those JOIN views let you build the appropriate cohort and then compute aggregates at that cohort grain (whereas movies_running_votes is fixed to partitioning by year only). | use movie_genre_counts(AGG) or movie_person_counts_by_role(AGG) when you need aggregated counts at the genre/person/role level — these AGG views produce properly aggregated rows and avoid the row-multiplication and double-counting risks that occur if you join movies_running_votes to JOIN views without re-aggregating.

views.description: Within-year cumulative sum of num_votes ordered by rating descending. Useful to analyze how vote accumulation relates to ranking within a year or to compute percentiles via joins. | Use for: Share of votes captured by top-N movies in a year; Cumulative distribution of votes by rating within a year
